title: Effect of quercetin supplementation on plasma lipid profiles ...
abstract:
## Abstract

Clinical trials examining the cardiovascular protective effects of quercetin in humans have reported conflicting results.

The aim of this systematic review was to summarize evidence of the effects of quercetin supplementation on plasma lipid profiles, blood pressure (BP), and glucose levels in humans by performing a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases were searched electronically from their inception to July 2018 to identify randomized controlled trials that assessed the impact of quercetin on lipid profiles, BP, and glucose levels.

Randomized controlled trials assessing the effects of quercetin or a standardized quercetin-enriched extract on plasma lipid profiles, BP, and glucose levels in humans were eligible for inclusion.
A random-effects model was used for data analysis. Continuous variables were expressed as weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95%CIs. Subgroup analyses were conducted to explore possible influences of study characteristics. Sensitivity analyses were also performed, as were analyses of publication bias.
Seventeen trials (n = 896 participants total) were included in the overall analysis. Pooled results showed that quercetin significantly lowered both systolic BP (WMD, −3.09 mmHg; 95%CI, −4.59 to −1.59; P = 0.0001) and diastolic BP (WMD, −2.86 mmHg; 95%CI, −5.09 to −0.63; P = 0.01).
Neither lipid profiles nor glucose concentrations changed significantly. In subgroup analyses, significant changes in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides were observed in trials with a parallel design and in which participants consumed quercetin for 8 weeks or more.

Quercetin intake resulted in significantly decreased BP in humans. Moreover, participants who consumed quercetin for 8 weeks or more showed significantly changed levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and triglycerides in trials with a parallel design.

This review aims to provide a snapshot of current knowledge about the clinical effects of quercetin in patients with CVD and to offer insights for future dietary recommendations to reduce CVD risk.

## METHODS

### Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Relevant studies were included if they satisfied the following criteria (Table 1): (1) quercetin or a standardized quercetin-enriched extract was investigated as a stand-alone intervention; (2) quercetin was administered for a period of 2 weeks or more; (3) the study was a randomized placebo-controlled clinical trial with either a crossover or a parallel trial design; (4) the study was conducted in adult participants (healthy or otherwise); (5) the study reported data on at least one of the designated outcome markers, ie, fasting blood glucose, triglycerides (TGs), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), LDL-C, total cholesterol, systolic BP (SBP), diastolic BP (DBP), insulin, and homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance (HOMA-IR); and (6) the study provided sufficient information on outcome markers both before and after the quercetin intervention in both control and treatment groups.

### Search strategy

The present meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines.

19 First, an in-depth systematic literature search was performed in the MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases from their inception to June 21, 2018. The search terms “quercetin” AND “3,3′,4′,5,7-pentahydroxylavone” were used as the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and related keywords. The search was limited to human studies and RCTs published in English. Reference lists of associated review articles identified during this process were also screened to identify additional studies in order to avoid missing any articles. All authors were involved in the screening of articles, with any disagreements discussed and resolved through consensus.

### Study quality and data extraction

Risk of bias and methodological quality were assessed independently by 2 authors using the Cochrane Collaboration’s risk assessment tool.

20 The following criteria were used to assess risk of bias: selective reporting, incomplete outcome data, blinding of outcome assessors, blinding of participants and study personnel, allocation concealment, randomization sequence generation, and other biases. The risk of bias in each study was labeled as unclear, high, or low, depending on the results for each criterion.

A predesigned data collection form was used to extract study characteristics and relevant results of selected RCTs. Discussions were held when disagreements arose. The following parameters were extracted from each study: publication year, first author’s name, location, demographic data (sex, mean age, health status, and baseline mean body mass index), study setting (number of patients enrolled and study design), intervention characteristics (including intervention duration, and formulation and dosage of quercetin supplement and placebo), and reported cardiovascular parameters. When multiple publications reported results for the same cohort or for a subsample of a participant cohort, information from the article that included the larger sample size was used. Data from the smaller study was included only if the larger study did not contain sufficient detail.

### Statistical analysis

In order to calculate the pooled effect sizes, continuous variables were expressed as weighted mean differences (WMDs) and 95%CIs. The

*I 2* statistic was used to quantify the degree of statistical heterogeneity between studies, with moderate to high heterogeneity recorded if this value exceeded 50%. 21Clinical heterogeneity was analyzed using a random-effects model. A traditional sensitivity analysis was also conducted to determine the impact of each study on the overall effect size by removing one study at a time and then reconducting the analysis. Predefined subgroup analyses and meta-regression analyses were carried out to investigate the potential moderating factors in the trials. The type of intervention, dosage of quercetin, trial duration, and study design were assessed for the subgroup analysis. Funnel plots, Begg rank correlation, and Egger weighted regression statistics were used to assess publication bias. 22 , 23STATA software (version 12.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX) and RevMan (version 5.0) software were used for statistical analyses. Two-tailed *P*values were used, with statistical significance conferred if the *P*value was less than 0.05, except where otherwise specified.
